Biology 30 · Chapter 17

Patterns and Processes in Inheritance

Alleles pass from parents to offspring through gametes. Use inheritance patterns, probability and pedigrees to explain how different allele combinations can produce different traits.

14 teaching topics1 integrated review15 required checks
Begin Topic 1

How traits are inherited

Alleles pass from parents to offspring through gametes. Use inheritance patterns, probability and pedigrees to explain how different allele combinations can produce different traits.

By the end of this chapter, I can:

  • I can translate genes and alleles into genotype and phenotype predictions.
  • I can solve single-trait, two-trait, ABO and sex-linked probability problems.
  • I can use pedigrees as evidence while preserving uncertainty.
  • I can interpret linkage data and genetic testing claims with appropriate limits.

Work through the topics, complete the required checks, and use the figures and practice activities to review. Your saved responses and vocabulary work are in Process Collection.

Genes, alleles, genotype and phenotype

How can the same gene be associated with different traits?

Learning goal

Distinguish a gene from an allele, genotype from phenotype, and homozygous from heterozygous combinations.

Before you begin

Homologous chromosomes carry corresponding genes but may carry different alleles. Gametes contribute one allele at each autosomal locus in the simple diploid model.

Chapter 17 · printed pp. 586–587

Open p. 586 · Open p. 587

Key terms: · · ·

Vocabulary help

Key terms

Words for this lesson

Use these definitions when you need help with a term.

A DNA sequence that contributes to a functional product or inherited characteristic.
An alternative version of a gene.
The allele combination an organism carries at the locus or loci being considered.
An observable or measurable characteristic resulting from genotype and its biological context.

Start with a defined genetic model

A is a DNA sequence associated with a functional product or characteristic. Alternative versions are alleles. In a diploid autosomal model, an individual inherits one from each parent and therefore has two alleles at the locus being studied.

The is the allele combination, such as BB, Bb or bb. The is the observed or measured characteristic, such as dark or pale pigment. A phenotype can also be an enzyme activity or another physiological property, not only a visible feature.

Dominance describes the heterozygote

Suppose a stated model says B gives dark pigment and is completely dominant to b. BB and Bb individuals have the dark phenotype, while bb individuals have the pale phenotype. The same phenotype can therefore correspond to more than one genotype.

Homozygous means the two alleles are the same, as in BB or bb. Heterozygous means they differ, as in Bb. A dominant allele is expressed in the heterozygote under the stated complete-dominance model. Dominant does not mean most common, healthiest or strongest.

Use the inheritance model supplied. Many traits involve multiple genes, environmental influences or allele relationships other than complete dominance. Do not assume that human eye colour can be accurately predicted by a single B/b model.

Notation keeps the reasoning visible

Define letters before solving a problem. Use the same letter for alleles of one gene and a different letter for a different gene. A capital and lowercase letter are convenient for a complete-dominance model; other models use different notation.

A useful first question is whether the phenotype determines a unique genotype. A recessive phenotype in a simple fully expressed model identifies bb. A dominant phenotype alone leaves BB or Bb possible. Keeping that uncertainty visible prevents an incorrect cross from the start.

Worked example

Infer what the phenotype does and does not tell you

In a fictional beetle model, dark shell B is completely dominant to pale shell b. One beetle is dark and another is pale.

  1. The pale beetle must be bb under this model.
  2. The dark beetle may be BB or Bb.
  3. Write B_ for the unresolved dark genotype rather than silently choosing BB.
  4. Additional parent or offspring information may resolve the missing allele.

Practise with support

Apply the explanation

Try both questions. Use the hint to revise your thinking after an incorrect answer.

Stop and think

Try this before opening the explanation

Is an allele a synonym for an entire chromosome?

Show the explanation

No. An allele is a version of a gene, which occupies a locus on a chromosome.

Mendel’s experiments and segregation

How can a trait disappear in one generation and reappear in the next?

Learning goal

Use P, F1 and F2 crosses to explain segregation of alleles without blending or loss of a recessive allele.

Before you begin

A heterozygote carries two different alleles. Under complete dominance, only one corresponding phenotype is apparent.

Chapter 17 · printed pp. 587–590

Open p. 587 · Open p. 590

Key terms: · · ·

Vocabulary help

Key terms

Words for this lesson

Use these definitions when you need help with a term.

The separation of the two alleles at a locus into different gametes.
Producing offspring with the same trait when bred within the line under the stated conditions.
The first offspring generation from a specified parental cross.
The generation produced from the F1 in the specified breeding design.

Follow the alleles across generations

Mendel studied traits in pea plants and used controlled crosses between lines with contrasting forms. In a simple example, let R represent round seeds and r wrinkled seeds, with complete dominance of R. A RR line crossed with rr produces Rr offspring in the .

Every F1 individual can have the round while still carrying the r . The recessive allele has not disappeared or blended into a weaker version. It remains part of the .

Segregation explains reappearance

An Rr individual forms gametes containing R or r. The alleles segregate as homologous chromosomes separate during meiosis. In the simple model, each allele has a one-half chance of entering a gamete.

When two Rr individuals produce the , gametes can combine as RR, Rr, rR or rr. Rr and rR name the same heterozygous genotype. The expected genotype ratio is 1 RR : 2 Rr : 1 rr. With complete dominance, the expected phenotype ratio is 3 round : 1 wrinkled.

The wrinkled phenotype reappears because an offspring can receive r from both parents. No new r mutation is required to explain that result.

Expected ratios are probabilities

A 3:1 expected ratio is not a promise that every group of four offspring contains exactly three round and one wrinkled. Each offspring is another event. Chance variation is especially noticeable in small samples.

Mendel's repeated patterns supported a particulate model of inheritance: inherited units remain distinguishable rather than permanently blending. Later chromosome and DNA evidence connected those units with cellular mechanisms.

When interpreting a cross, identify the parental genotypes, gamete possibilities and allele combinations before applying the phenotype rule. A remembered ratio should be the result of that reasoning, not a substitute for it.

Worked example

Recover a hidden allele

A true-breeding dark plant is crossed with a true-breeding pale plant. All F1 plants are dark; some F2 offspring are pale.

  1. Under complete dominance, use DD for the true-breeding dark parent and dd for pale.
  2. The F1 genotype is Dd. The d allele remains present despite the dark phenotype.
  3. F1 parents can each contribute d in a gamete.
  4. An F2 dd offspring expresses pale, explaining reappearance without blending or a new mutation.

Practise with support

Apply the explanation

Try both questions. Use the hint to revise your thinking after an incorrect answer.

Stop and think

Try this before opening the explanation

Does a recessive allele have to be visible to remain inherited?

Show the explanation

No. A heterozygote can carry an allele whose recessive phenotype is not expressed.

How do you turn parental genotypes into an offspring prediction?

Learning goal

Construct and interpret a monohybrid Punnett square, distinguish genotype and phenotype probabilities, and state the denominator.

Chapter 17 · printed pp. 589–591

Open p. 589 · Open p. 591

Key terms: · · ·

Vocabulary help

Key terms

Words for this lesson

Use these definitions when you need help with a term.

A table combining possible parental gametes to organize offspring genotypes.
A cross between individuals heterozygous for one studied gene.
The expected proportion of an outcome under specified conditions.
The predicted count obtained by multiplying a probability by the sample size.

Write gametes, not whole parental genotypes, on the edges

A organizes combinations of gametes. For Aa × aa, the first parent produces A or a gametes; the second produces only a. Place those gametes on the edges and combine one from each parent in each cell.

The resulting possibilities are Aa and aa in equal proportions. With complete dominance, half are expected to have the dominant and half the recessive phenotype. The square shows why the 1:1 ratio applies; a 3:1 ratio would be the wrong shortcut for this cross.

Count the outcome that was actually asked for

For Aa × Aa, the four equally likely combinations are AA, Aa, aA and aa. Grouping the two heterozygous combinations gives probabilities of 1/4 AA, 1/2 Aa and 1/4 aa. The dominant phenotype has 3/4 under complete dominance.

probability and phenotype probability therefore can differ. “Heterozygous” refers to two of the four combinations, while “dominant phenotype” includes three. Mark the requested group before choosing your numerator.

When converting to an , multiply by the total. If 80 offspring each have a 1/4 chance of aa, the expected number is 80 × 0.25 = 20. The result is an expectation, not a promise.

Independent offspring do not compensate for earlier outcomes

In the simple model, one offspring's genotype does not force the next offspring to be different. If two Aa parents have several dominant-phenotype offspring, the modeled probability for the next offspring is still 1/4 recessive.

For specified independent events, multiply probabilities. Two recessive offspring in a row from Aa × Aa have probability 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16. Do not confuse this ordered event with “at least one recessive among two,” which asks for a different set of outcomes.

State assumptions such as complete dominance and ordinary segregation. They determine which genotype combinations count toward a phenotype.

Worked example

Predict a phenotype and an expected count

In a stated complete-dominance model, Tt is crossed with tt. Predict the fraction and expected number of recessive offspring among 60.

  1. Tt produces T and t gametes; tt produces t gametes.
  2. The equally likely combinations are Tt and tt.
  3. The recessive phenotype is tt, probability 1/2.
  4. Expected number = 60 × 1/2 = 30.
  5. Check: the other expected 30 have the dominant phenotype; observed counts can vary.

Practise with support

Apply the explanation

Try both questions. Use the hint to revise your thinking after an incorrect answer.

Stop and think

Try this before opening the explanation

Why should the square’s edges contain A or a rather than Aa?

Show the explanation

The edges represent gametes, which carry one allele at the studied locus.

Chapter 17 · printed pp. 590–591

Open p. 590 · Open p. 591

Key terms: · · ·

Vocabulary help

Key terms

Words for this lesson

Use these definitions when you need help with a term.

A cross with a homozygous recessive individual used to investigate an unknown genotype.
Having two identical alleles at a locus.
Having two different alleles at a locus.
Differences between observed sample outcomes and their expected proportions due to chance.

Choose a tester with a known contribution

An individual with a dominant may be AA or Aa. Crossing it with aa creates a useful test because the recessive tester can contribute only a. The phenotype of the offspring then provides evidence about the unknown parent's contribution.

If the unknown parent is AA, every offspring is expected to be Aa and show the dominant phenotype. If the unknown parent is Aa, the expected offspring are half Aa and half aa. A recessive offspring therefore demonstrates that the unknown parent contributed a, under the stated simple model.

Positive evidence and absence of evidence differ

One aa offspring from B_ × bb means the dominant-phenotype parent must carry the recessive , assuming the model, parentage and observations are correct. It is .

By contrast, several dominant offspring do not logically prove the parent is . An Aa parent can, by chance, produce a run of A-bearing gametes. For four independent offspring in an Aa × aa cross, the that all show the dominant phenotype is (1/2)⁴ = 1/16.

More offspring with no recessive phenotype generally strengthen the homozygous interpretation, but finite samples still require cautious wording. Say what the evidence supports and what remains possible.

Use family information before calculating

Additional parent or offspring information can resolve an unknown . A dominant-phenotype individual with an aa parent must have received a from that parent, so it must be Aa. You do not need another to establish that conclusion within the model.

Start with the most informative constraints. Write the alleles that must be present, preserve unknowns where necessary, and only then calculate the next cross. Guessing an unresolved genotype can make every later arithmetic step misleading.

Worked example

A recessive offspring resolves the unknown

A black fictional mouse, B_, is crossed with a brown bb mouse. One offspring is brown.

  1. The brown offspring is bb.
  2. The known tester supplied one b.
  3. The unknown black parent supplied the other b, so it carries b.
  4. Its black phenotype also requires B in the complete-dominance model.
  5. The unknown parent is Bb.

Chapter 17 · printed pp. 591–593

Open p. 591 · Open p. 593

Key terms: · · ·

Vocabulary help

Key terms

Words for this lesson

Use these definitions when you need help with a term.

A cross between individuals heterozygous at two studied loci.
Independent segregation of alleles at different loci when the chromosome arrangement permits it.
Multiplication of probabilities for specified independent events.
The set of one allele from each studied locus carried by a gamete.

Find possible gametes before drawing boxes

For AaBb with , choose one from the A/a pair and one from the B/b pair. The possible gametes are AB, Ab, aB and ab, each with 1/4. An Aabb parent has only Ab and ab as distinct possibilities.

Do not place Aa or Bb on a gamete edge. Those are two alleles of one locus, not one allele from each of two loci. A correctly sized square follows from the distinct gametes, not from a rule that every two-trait cross needs sixteen boxes.

Solve separate loci when independence is stated

For AaBb × AaBb, the A locus gives a 3/4 dominant- probability and 1/4 recessive probability. The B locus gives the same. If the loci assort independently, the probability of both dominant phenotypes is 3/4 × 3/4 = 9/16.

The other phenotype combinations are 3/16, 3/16 and 1/16, producing the familiar 9:3:3:1 expectation. This ratio is specific to the stated heterozygote cross and allele relationships.

For a different cross, recompute. In AaBb × aaBb, probability of A_ is 1/2 and probability of B_ is 3/4, so both dominant phenotypes have probability 3/8. A memorized 9/16 would be wrong.

Make the assumption part of the answer

Genes close together on the same chromosome can be linked. Their gamete combinations may not occur equally, so the simple product calculation can fail. Later lessons will use offspring data to test this.

For now, state when independent assortment is assumed. Check that the probabilities of all mutually exclusive phenotype categories add to one. When calculating an expected count, multiply the appropriate probability by the total number of offspring.

Both the square and product method are tools for organizing the same biological possibilities. Choose the clearer method, but show enough steps that the allele contributions can be checked.

Worked example

Solve a two-locus cross without unnecessary boxes

In an independent complete-dominance model, RrTt × rrTt produces offspring. Find the probability of red, short offspring: R_tt.

  1. At the colour locus, Rr × rr gives P(R_) = 1/2.
  2. At the height locus, Tt × Tt gives P(tt) = 1/4.
  3. Both conditions are required, so multiply: 1/2 × 1/4 = 1/8.
  4. For 80 offspring the expected count is 80 × 1/8 = 10.
  5. The result relies on independence of the two loci.

Show the explanation

No. Parental genotypes, dominance relationships and linkage determine the prediction.

How can a heterozygote differ from either homozygote?

Chapter 17 · printed pp. 594–598

Open p. 594 · Open p. 598

Key terms: · · ·

Vocabulary help

Key terms

Words for this lesson

Use these definitions when you need help with a term.

An allele relationship in which the heterozygote has an intermediate phenotype.
An allele relationship in which both allele-associated products or traits are expressed in a heterozygote.
The characteristic expressed when two different alleles occur together.
The expected relative proportions of expressed trait categories.

The alleles still segregate

Under , the heterozygote has an intermediate . In a stated flower model, R1R1 is red, R2R2 is white and R1R2 is pink. The alleles remain R1 and R2; they have not permanently fused into a pink .

Crossing two pink R1R2 plants gives R1R1, R1R2, R2R1 and R2R2 combinations. Grouped genotypes occur in a 1:2:1 ratio. Because all three genotypes have distinguishable phenotypes, the phenotype ratio is also 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white.

Both expressed is different from intermediate

In , both allele-associated products or characteristics are expressed in the heterozygote. In a roan cattle model, red and white hairs are both present rather than becoming uniformly pink hair. In ABO blood groups, both A and B antigens can be expressed on red blood cells.

Do not define codominance only as different cells expressing different alleles. The essential idea is detectable expression of both allele contributions. The way that expression appears depends on the trait.

Use superscripts or clear allele labels such as R1 and R2 when neither allele is treated as completely dominant. Define the notation before interpreting the cross.

Change the phenotype rule, not the whole inheritance process

Punnett-square construction works the same way: list one allele per gamete, combine the possibilities, then use the specified -to-phenotype rule. The difference from complete dominance lies in the heterozygote's phenotype.

A 1:2:1 genotype ratio can therefore produce either a 3:1 phenotype ratio under complete dominance or a 1:2:1 phenotype ratio when the three genotypes are distinguishable. The ratio alone must be read alongside the model.

Avoid calling one relationship “stronger” or “more advanced.” These are descriptions of expression, not rankings of alleles.

Worked example

Compare the same genotype cross under two models

R1R2 × R1R2 is used in one incomplete-dominance flower model and one codominant coat-colour model.

  1. The genotype probabilities are 1/4 R1R1, 1/2 R1R2 and 1/4 R2R2 in both.
  2. In incomplete dominance, the heterozygote is intermediate, such as pink.
  3. In codominance, both contributions are expressed, such as red and white hairs.
  4. The allele-segregation calculation stays the same; the interpretation of R1R2 changes.

Practise with support

Apply the explanation

Try both questions. Use the hint to revise your thinking after an incorrect answer.

Stop and think

Try this before opening the explanation

Do incomplete dominance and codominance cancel Mendel’s segregation rule?

Show the explanation

No. They change how allele combinations are expressed, not the one-allele contribution of each gamete.

Chapter 17 · printed pp. 596–598

Open p. 596 · Open p. 598

Key terms: · · ·

Vocabulary help

Key terms

Words for this lesson

Use these definitions when you need help with a term.

More than two allele versions of one gene present in a population.
A blood-group system modeled with IA, IB and i alleles producing A, B, AB and O phenotypes.
Alleles whose contributions are both expressed in the heterozygote.
An individual who carries a recessive disease-associated allele without expressing the recessive condition in a specified simple model.

Population diversity is not individual copy number

A population can contain many versions of a . Each diploid individual still usually inherits two alleles at an autosomal locus, one from each parent. refers to the range of versions in the population, not three or more copies in every individual.

The simplified ABO model uses IA, IB and i. IA contributes A antigen expression; IB contributes B antigen expression; i does not produce either A or B antigen in this model. IA and IB are codominant, and each is dominant over i.

Connect each phenotype to possible genotypes

Type A can be IAIA or IAi. Type B can be IBIB or IBi. Type AB is IAIB, and type O is ii in the standard model. The phenotypes A and B leave uncertainty unless additional family information is available.

An individual with type B and a type O parent must have inherited i from that parent. Therefore the type B individual's genotype is IBi. This is the same constraint reasoning used in a .

Use clear notation. IAIB represents two alleles of one gene, not four separate genes. In plain text, write IA and IB consistently and keep the pairs grouped.

Calculate from the actual cross

For IAi × IBi, possible offspring genotypes are IAIB, IAi, IBi and ii, each with 1/4. The four ABO phenotypes are therefore each possible with probability 1/4 in this specific cross.

A different cross gives different predictions. IAIA × IBi produces IAIB and IAi, each with probability 1/2; no ii offspring is possible because the first parent cannot contribute i.

These models teach inheritance and probability. Real blood typing includes additional factors and rare variants. Do not use a classroom square as a clinical transfusion rule or as definitive proof of family relationships.

Worked example

Use family information before the square

A type B parent has a type O father. This parent has a child with a type AB partner. Find the probability of type O.

  1. The type O father is ii and supplies i, so the type B parent is IBi.
  2. The AB partner is IAIB and can supply IA or IB, but not i.
  3. An O child would require ii.
  4. Because one parent cannot supply i, the probability is 0 in the simplified model.

Apply the explanation

Try both questions. Use the hint to revise your thinking after an incorrect answer.

Try this before opening the explanation

Show the explanation

Chapter 17 · printed pp. 601–605

Open p. 601 · Open p. 605

Key terms: · · ·

Vocabulary help

Key terms

Words for this lesson

Use these definitions when you need help with a term.

Located on the X chromosome.
Having only one copy of a gene in the relevant chromosome context.
Probability calculated within a stated subgroup or condition.
An inheritance model in which the recessive allele is on X and is expressed in a hemizygous XY individual.

Keep alleles attached to their chromosomes

Use X superscripts or clear plain-text forms such as XB and Xb. In a typical XX/XY model, an XX parent contributes an X to every offspring; an XY parent contributes X or Y. Many loci have no corresponding on Y.

For a simple condition, XbY expresses the condition because there is no second X-linked allele to mask it. XBXb can be an unaffected under the stated complete-expression assumptions, while XbXb is affected. These are inheritance models, not a complete account of every variation in sex development or expression.

Use the cross to find the correct denominator

Consider XBXb × XBY. The four equally likely combinations are XBXB, XBXb, XBY and XbY. One of four children is expected to be affected. Among sons only, one of two is expected to be affected.

The of “a son who is affected” is 1/4 among all children. The probability that “the next son is affected” is 1/2 conditional on being a son. The wording changes the denominator, not the biological cross.

An affected father passes his X chromosome to daughters and his Y to sons in this model. Father-to-son transmission therefore is not expected for an X-linked allele through that direct chromosome path.

Separate recessive and dominant X-linked models

For a simple fully penetrant X-linked dominant trait, an affected father with an unaffected partner passes his affected X to every daughter and to no son. An affected mother can pass the allele to either sons or daughters.

These patterns are useful evidence, but a small family may not contain every possible outcome. Later pedigree lessons will require testing candidate explanations against the whole family rather than treating one clue as proof.

Always define allele meaning, parental genotypes and the subgroup asked about before calculating.

Worked example

Answer two similar-looking questions

A carrier XAXa mother and unaffected XAY father have children in a simple X-linked recessive model.

  1. List the four equally likely combinations: XAXA, XAXa, XAY and XaY.
  2. Affected child: XaY is one of four, so probability = 1/4.
  3. Affected among sons: XaY is one of two son outcomes, so probability = 1/2.
  4. A son who is affected among all children: probability remains 1/4.
  5. Write the denominator in words to show which question you answered.

Practise with support

Apply the explanation

Try both questions. Use the hint to revise your thinking after an incorrect answer.

Why should an X-linked cross retain X and Y in the notation?

Show the explanation

Chapter 17 · printed pp. 606–609

Open p. 606 · Open p. 609

Key terms: · · ·

Vocabulary help

Key terms

Words for this lesson

Use these definitions when you need help with a term.

Inheritance in which multiple genes contribute to a trait.
A range of phenotype values without only a few sharply separated categories.
An effect of conditions such as nutrition or temperature on phenotype.
Use of genetic information to produce functional products in cells.

Several genes can contribute to one measurement

A polygenic trait is influenced by multiple genes. Different combinations across these loci can produce a range of outcomes. Human height and many aspects of pigmentation are examples of traits that are not adequately represented by one complete-dominance pair.

describes measurements spread over a range. It does not require every possible value, nor does it prove that environment is the only influence. Many combinations and environmental conditions can together generate a broad distribution.

The environment affects expression and development

Nutrition, temperature and other conditions can influence a . Plants with similar genotypes may reach different heights under different light or nutrient conditions. The measured difference does not automatically establish a difference in DNA sequence.

describes which genetic information is used and how much product is made. Cells with the same inherited genome can have different functions because they express different sets of genes. Environmental or developmental signals can change expression.

Some regulatory changes involve chemical modifications associated with DNA or chromatin. These are often discussed as epigenetic changes. Do not treat every such change as a mutation or assume it is always inherited through many generations.

Ask what the evidence separates

If two groups differ in both and environment, a phenotype difference cannot be assigned to either factor alone without additional evidence. Controlled comparisons hold relevant conditions constant or use designs that help separate contributions.

A genetic association can indicate a relationship without determining an individual outcome with certainty. Many traits and conditions involve multiple factors. The existence of a risk-associated allele is not equivalent to an inevitable phenotype.

For a course answer, name the proposed contributions, identify what was measured and explain the limit. Avoid forcing a complex trait into a single-gene square just because that calculation is familiar.

Worked example

Interpret an environmental comparison

Genetically similar cuttings are grown under high or low light, with other measured conditions kept similar. Their average growth differs.

  1. The genetic similarity reduces one source of variation.
  2. The light condition differs systematically, so it is a plausible contributor.
  3. The result concerns growth under those conditions; it does not prove a new allele appeared.
  4. Check replication and other controlled conditions before making a stronger causal claim.

Try both questions. Use the hint to revise your thinking after an incorrect answer.

Try this before opening the explanation

Should a risk-associated genotype always be treated as a guaranteed outcome?

Show the explanation

No. Penetrance, environment and other genetic factors can influence the outcome.

Vocabulary help

Key terms

Words for this lesson

Use these definitions when you need help with a term.

A diagram tracing a specified trait through family relationships across generations.
A model in which a trait is expressed when two recessive alleles occur at an autosomal locus.
A model in which one dominant allele at an autosomal locus is sufficient for expression under the stated assumptions.
A level of descent in a family diagram, commonly labelled with a Roman numeral.

Read the diagram before solving it

A uses symbols and connecting lines to represent family relationships and a specified trait. Conventional squares and circles often represent male and female individuals in the model; shading indicates expression of the trait. A key should explain any additional symbols.

Roman numerals identify generations and ordinary numbers identify individuals within a . A label such as II-3 refers to the third numbered individual in generation II. Follow the parent–offspring line carefully; neighbouring symbols are not automatically siblings or partners.

Use required allele contributions

For an model, affected individuals are aa. Two unaffected parents with an affected child must each contribute a. If both are unaffected, each is therefore Aa under the simple fully penetrant model.

For an model, unaffected individuals are dd. An affected parent with an unaffected child must be able to contribute d, so that affected parent is Dd rather than DD. The child's constrains the parent's possible alleles.

These deductions use the stated model, accurate relationships and complete expression. New mutations, reduced penetrance or other complexities can change the interpretation; do not add them silently to a simple problem.

Leave uncertainty where it belongs

An unaffected sibling of an aa child from Aa × Aa can be AA or Aa. Excluding aa leaves three equally likely genotype combinations: AA, Aa and aA. Therefore the that an unaffected sibling is a is 2/3, not 1/2, under this cross.

Do not assign AA simply because a person is unshaded. Write the allowed alternatives unless other evidence resolves them. The distinction between “must be” and “could be” is important.

A pedigree can make some genotypes certain within a model while leaving others unresolved. A good explanation identifies the relative whose contribution provides the evidence.

Worked example

Infer both parents from a recessive child

Two unaffected parents have an affected child in a fully penetrant autosomal recessive model.

  1. The affected child is aa and needs a from each parent.
  2. Each unaffected parent must also carry A.
  3. Therefore both parents are Aa.
  4. An unaffected sibling may be AA or Aa; do not automatically mark that sibling as a carrier.
  5. Conditional on being unaffected, the carrier probability is 2/3 for this parental cross.

Show the explanation

How can you test an inheritance explanation against an entire family?

Learning goal

Use chromosome transmission to evaluate X-linked models and distinguish consistency from proof in small pedigrees.

Before you begin

In the typical XX/XY model, fathers pass X to daughters and Y to sons. A small family may not show every possible outcome.

Chapter 17 · printed pp. 613–617

Open p. 613 · Open p. 617

Key terms: · · ·

Vocabulary help

Key terms

Words for this lesson

Use these definitions when you need help with a term.

A simple model in which a dominant allele on X produces the trait under specified penetrance assumptions.
The proportion of individuals with a genotype who express the associated phenotype.
A possible inheritance explanation tested against the observed relationships and traits.
An individual who must carry a recessive allele under the stated pedigree model.

Trace the chromosome, not only the shading pattern

For inheritance, follow which parent supplies X to each offspring. Sons receive their X from their mother in the typical XX/XY model. Daughters receive one X from each parent. Fathers do not directly pass an X-linked to sons.

In a fully penetrant model, an affected son has XbY. His Xb came from his mother. An unaffected mother must therefore be XBXb under the ordinary no-new-mutation assumptions. An affected daughter needs Xb from both parents, which constrains the father's .

Compare dominant and recessive X-linked patterns

An affected father in an model passes the affected X to every daughter. With an unaffected mother, sons receive the father's Y and the mother's unaffected X, so they are unaffected under that model.

For X-linked recessive inheritance, an affected father with a unaffected mother has daughters and unaffected sons. The same chromosome route produces a different expressed pattern because the differs.

More affected males can be a clue to an X-linked recessive model, but sex counts alone are not decisive. A small autosomal family can also show an uneven distribution by chance.

Look for contradictions and retain limits

A strong analysis tests every informative relationship. A model may fit one branch but fail elsewhere. Use “consistent with” when the evidence supports a model without uniquely proving it.

State assumptions: complete , ordinary chromosome transmission, accurate parentage and no newly arising mutations unless specified. These simplify the question and make deductions possible. Real clinical pedigrees can require more evidence.

When calculating the risk to a future child, establish the relevant parents' genotypes first and read the requested subgroup. The pedigree does not remove the distinction between among sons and probability among all children.

Worked example

Test a proposed X-linked recessive model

A fully expressed recessive trait appears in a daughter whose father is unaffected. Assume ordinary XX/XY transmission and no new mutation.

  1. An affected daughter would need XbXb in this model.
  2. Her father must supply one of those Xb chromosomes.
  3. An unaffected father is XBY and cannot supply Xb under the assumptions.
  4. The proposed model is inconsistent with this relationship; another explanation or changed assumptions would be needed.

Chapter 17 · printed pp. 599–601

Open p. 599 · Open p. 601

Key terms: · · ·

Vocabulary help

Key terms

Words for this lesson

Use these definitions when you need help with a term.

Genes on the same chromosome that may be inherited together, especially when close.
An allele combination matching one of the original chromosome arrangements in the heterozygous parent.
An allele combination different from the parent’s original arrangement for the loci considered.
The arrangement of alleles across the two homologous chromosomes.

A genotype can hide chromosome arrangement

AaBb tells you which alleles are present but not how they are arranged on the homologues. AB/ab places A with B on one chromosome and a with b on the other. Ab/aB places A with b and a with B. This arrangement is called .

The original combinations are parental. Crossing over between the loci can generate recombinant combinations. Which combinations count as parental therefore depends on the starting arrangement, not simply whether the letters are both uppercase.

A test cross can reveal gamete combinations

Cross a heterozygote with aabb. The tester contributes only ab, so the offspring's or can reveal the heterozygote's gamete contribution. Under , the four combinations are expected in equal proportions.

If the heterozygote has AB/ab and the genes are linked, AB and ab gametes often occur more frequently than Ab and aB. The corresponding parental offspring classes are larger, and the recombinant classes smaller.

Read the actual counts, not just the presence of four categories. can produce all four combinations if crossing over occurs, but the proportions can differ from 1:1:1:1.

Linkage is about probability, not an absolute lock

Closer genes are less likely to be separated by crossing over between them. Genes farther apart may show more recombination. Multiple crossovers can complicate the relationship between observed recombinant frequency and physical distance.

A small sample can depart from equal counts by chance, so a slight imbalance alone is not conclusive proof of linkage. Large, consistent differences provide stronger evidence under the stated model.

Keep the explanation at the correct level: crossing over changes combinations within chromosomes, and offspring counts can provide evidence about those gamete combinations.

Worked example

Identify parental and recombinant classes

An AB/ab heterozygote is crossed with ab/ab. Offspring reveal 42 AB, 40 ab, 9 Ab and 9 aB gamete contributions.

  1. The stated parental phase is AB/ab, so AB and ab are parental.
  2. Ab and aB are recombinant combinations.
  3. There are 82 parental and 18 recombinant observations among 100.
  4. The excess parental classes is consistent with linkage in this model.
  5. The counts do not mean only 18 cells underwent any crossing over anywhere; they concern the two loci being scored.

Chapter 17 · printed pp. 599–601

Open p. 599 · Open p. 601

Key terms: · · ·

Vocabulary help

Key terms

Words for this lesson

Use these definitions when you need help with a term.

The fraction of scored offspring or gametes that are recombinant for the loci considered.
A unit of genetic map distance corresponding approximately to one percent recombination over short intervals.
A map of relative gene order and distances estimated from recombination data.
Two exchange events within a chromosome region.

Calculate the fraction carefully

equals recombinant observations divided by total scored observations, multiplied by 100%. In a , add both reciprocal recombinant classes. Do not divide only by the parental classes or by one quarter of the offspring.

For 84 parental class 1, 76 parental class 2, 22 recombinant class 1 and 18 recombinant class 2, the total is 200. Recombinants total 40. Frequency = 40/200 × 100% = 20%.

In a simple short-interval model, this suggests approximately 20 map units between the loci. The result is a relative genetic distance estimate, not an exact physical measurement.

Use three distances to infer order

Suppose A–B is 6 map units, B–C is 14 and A–C is 20 in a simple additive map. Since 6 + 14 = 20, B lies between A and C. Either A—6—B—14—C or its reversed orientation expresses the same relative order.

Two distances alone may leave more than one order possible. Place the genes tentatively and ask what additional comparison would distinguish the alternatives. Do not invent a third distance merely to finish the drawing.

Understand the limits of two-locus data

Observed recombination frequency approaches 50% for independently assorting loci or sufficiently separated loci. It does not provide an unbounded direct ruler. Multiple crossovers can restore parental outside-marker combinations, so some exchange events are not detected by scoring only two loci.

A chromosome map can span more than 50 map units when shorter intervals are combined, even though a two-locus recombination fraction does not rise above the independent limit in the standard model. These are different quantities.

The connection between centimorgans and base pairs varies across regions and organisms. Report the calculated genetic distance and assumptions, rather than converting every into one fixed DNA length.

Worked example

Calculate frequency and check the denominator

A test cross gives parental counts 90 and 86 and recombinant counts 12 and 12.

  1. Total offspring = 90 + 86 + 12 + 12 = 200.
  2. Recombinants = 12 + 12 = 24.
  3. Frequency = 24/200 = 0.12 = 12%.
  4. Short-interval map estimate: about 12 cM.
  5. Reasonableness check: recombinant classes are less common than parental classes, and 12% is below 50%.

Practise with support

Apply the explanation

Try both questions. Use the hint to revise your thinking after an incorrect answer.

Stop and think

Try this before opening the explanation

Show the explanation

No. Recheck parental-class assignment, counts and model assumptions; the standard two-locus limit is 50%.

Chapter 17 · printed pp. 610–617

Open p. 610 · Open p. 617

Key terms: · · ·

Vocabulary help

Key terms

Words for this lesson

Use these definitions when you need help with a term.

Analysis of genetic material or related markers to investigate particular variants or conditions.
A process helping people understand genetic information, inheritance and possible implications for their choices.
Agreement based on understanding the purpose, potential benefits, risks and alternatives of a procedure or study.
A probability or increased likelihood associated with genetic information in a specified context.

Read the scope of the test

A genetic test investigates particular variants, regions or markers. A result must be interpreted within that scope. A negative result for one variant does not rule out every genetic cause of a trait or condition.

Some results are strongly predictive under a clear inheritance model. Others indicate an increased or remain uncertain. , other genes, environment and the quality of the evidence can influence what a result means for an individual.

Information can affect more than one person

A result can have implications for relatives because family members share some genetic information. A person may wish to know a result, decline it or discuss its meaning before deciding how to use it. helps explain inheritance, limitations and possible implications.

Consent should address what is tested, what results may be returned and how samples or data may be used. Privacy and access to information are relevant concerns. This chapter examines those issues without giving legal advice or assuming one personal choice is appropriate for everyone.

A scientific explanation should separate observed data, estimated risk and value-based decisions. An association does not itself prescribe how a person should act.

Evaluate a claim using evidence and uncertainty

Suppose a hypothetical test reports a variant associated with a higher risk of a condition. Ask which population was studied, how large the increase is, what other factors matter and whether the result has been validated for the proposed use.

A claim that one result predicts every future feature of a person's health goes beyond the evidence. Conversely, uncertainty does not mean the information has no value. The useful task is to identify what the result can support and what additional evidence or counselling is needed.

Classroom case studies should not require students to reveal their own family history or test information. Use the supplied fictional scenarios for analysis.

Worked example

Interpret a limited negative result

A fictional test detects none of three specified variants associated with one condition.

  1. The result establishes that those tested variants were not detected under the test’s conditions.
  2. It does not rule out every untested variant, every different genetic condition or every environmental cause.
  3. Interpretation requires the test’s scope and limitations.
  4. A personal decision should be informed by appropriate counselling rather than a blanket classroom rule.

No. Fictional cases can teach the reasoning without requiring personal disclosure.

Key terms

Words for this lesson

Use these definitions when you need help with a term.

The allele combination an organism carries at the locus or loci being considered.
The expected proportion of an outcome under specified conditions.
A diagram tracing a specified trait through family relationships across generations.
The fraction of scored offspring or gametes that are recombinant for the loci considered.

One method, several inheritance models

Begin with the gene or genes, the allele relationships and parental genotypes. Segregation determines the allele contribution of gametes; the phenotype model determines which offspring combinations express the trait. Complete dominance, incomplete dominance, codominance and X-linkage change how outcomes are interpreted.

A two-locus product calculation requires independence. A linked model instead uses phase and recombinant frequencies. A pedigree adds constraints from relatives but may leave more than one genotype or inheritance model possible.

Show the denominator and the limit

Probability among all children differs from probability among sons or among unaffected siblings. Count the requested subgroup explicitly. Multiply independent required events, and convert a probability to an expected count only after establishing the correct cross.

Expected ratios are not guarantees for small samples. Genetic associations are not always deterministic predictions. A complete answer gives both the result and the conditions under which it follows.

Connect the main ideas

TopicWhat you should be able to explain
Genes, alleles, genotype and phenotypeDistinguish a gene from an allele, genotype from phenotype, and homozygous from heterozygous combinations.
Mendel’s experiments and segregationUse P, F1 and F2 crosses to explain segregation of alleles without blending or loss of a recessive allele.
Single-trait crosses and probabilityConstruct and interpret a monohybrid Punnett square, distinguish genotype and phenotype probabilities, and state the denominator.
Test crosses and unknown genotypesUse a homozygous recessive tester to distinguish possible parental genotypes and explain uncertainty from small samples.
Two-trait crosses and independent assortmentList valid gametes for two loci, use a Punnett square or product rule, and identify the assumption of independent assortment.
Incomplete dominance and codominanceCompare incomplete dominance and codominance while preserving ordinary allele segregation.
Multiple alleles and ABO blood groupsUse the ABO model to distinguish population allele diversity from individual genotype and solve blood-group crosses.
Sex-linked inheritanceUse a typical XX/XY model to solve X-linked crosses and distinguish conditional from joint probabilities.
Polygenic traits and environmental influencesExplain polygenic and environmental contributions, and distinguish genotype, gene expression and measured phenotype.
Reading autosomal pedigreesRead pedigree symbols and generations, infer autosomal genotypes under a stated model, and preserve unresolved alternatives.
Sex-linked pedigrees and testing a modelUse chromosome transmission to evaluate X-linked models and distinguish consistency from proof in small pedigrees.
Linked genes and recombinant offspringIdentify linked allele arrangements, parental and recombinant combinations, and use a test cross to interpret gamete frequencies.
Recombination frequency and chromosome mapsCalculate recombination frequency, construct simple maps and distinguish map distance from a universal physical base-pair distance.
Genetic testing, counselling and decisionsDistinguish a genetic test result from a guaranteed phenotype, and identify consent, uncertainty and privacy considerations.

Worked example

Compare probability and linkage evidence

A two-locus test cross has four phenotype classes but parental classes are much larger. A student applies 1:1:1:1 without examining the counts.

  1. The 1:1:1:1 prediction assumes independent assortment.
  2. Identify the parental chromosome arrangement and classify both recombinant groups.
  3. Compare observed counts with the independent expectation, considering sampling.
  4. Calculate recombination frequency from both recombinant groups over the whole sample.
  5. Use a justified model rather than forcing every cross into a memorized ratio.

Written explanations

Written explanation 1

Maximum 3200 characters. Explain the biology in your own words.

Compare after saving your own response

Define alleles and the inheritance model. Infer parental genotypes using phenotype and family evidence, preserving unresolved alternatives. List gametes, combine them by an appropriate square or independent product rule, identify the requested subgroup and calculate with the correct denominator. Interpret the result as an expectation and state assumptions.

Check your explanation for:
  • Identifies the relevant structures or quantities.
  • Explains the causal relationship or calculation, not just the final result.
  • Uses the stated evidence and avoids a stronger conclusion than it supports.

Written explanation 2

Maximum 3200 characters. Explain the biology in your own words.

Compare after saving your own response

Under independence a heterozygote test cross can yield four equal classes. Linked loci can produce more parental than recombinant combinations. Identify phase, sum both recombinant classes, divide by all scored offspring and multiply by 100%. For short intervals this approximates map distance, with limitations from multiple crossovers and sampling.

Optional textbook practice for Chapter review and final check

Optional extension

Biobanks and genetic information

What does a shared genetic database need to make a finding meaningful?

Shared data can support research

A biobank stores biological samples and associated information for research. Comparing many samples can help investigate relationships between variants, environments and phenotypes.

Consider a hypothetical study that finds a variant more often in one group than another. The groups also differ in age and sampling location. The association is a starting point, not proof that the variant alone causes the phenotype.

Evaluate evidence and participation

Researchers need to consider sampling, confounding variables, validation and how results generalize. Participants also need clear information about consent, data use, access and possible family implications.

The case asks you to distinguish scientific interpretation from decisions about participation. No personal sample, family history or disclosure is required.

Save an optional explanation

This is optional written practice. It does not change required progress.

Optional response. Select Save response to collect it. Maximum 5000 characters.

Compare after saving your explanation

The groups differ in age and location, so the association may be affected by confounding or population structure and requires further validation. Participants should understand how samples and information will be used or shared and what choices they retain. Neither issue is resolved by merely collecting more DNA.

  • Explains the causal relationship or calculation, not just the final result.
  • Uses the stated evidence and avoids a stronger conclusion than it supports.
